title: Impossibility of Perfectly Complete Many-Round Key Agreement in the QROM
authors: Longcheng Li, Qian Li, Xingjian Li, Qipeng Liu
abstract: This paper proves that it is impossible to construct perfectly complete quantum key agreement protocols (QKA) from quantumly secure one-way functions (OWFs) in a black-box manner.   Specifically, consider any protocol in which Alice and Bob exchange only classical messages, make at most $q_{\mathsf{A}}$ and $q_{\mathsf{B}}$ quantum queries, respectively, to a Boolean-valued random oracle, and agree on a shared key with certainty. This paper shows that there exists an eavesdropper, given the classical messages, that can recover the shared key with certainty using $O((q_{\mathsf{A}}+q_{\mathsf{B}})^5)$ classical oracle queries. The bound is independent of the number of rounds, transcript length, key length, and oracle-domain size. Previous results only applies to two-round key agreement (Li et al. CRYPTO 26) or relies on unproven conjectures (Austrin et al. CRYPTO 22).   GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra found this proof in a one-shot conversation and drafted a preliminary version of this paper. summary: This theoretical paper proves a strong impossibility result showing that perfectly complete Quantum Key Agreement (QKA) protocols cannot be built from black-box one-way functions. The authors show an eavesdropper can always recover the key efficiently by exploiting the structure imposed by perfect completeness within the QROM model. This work significantly tightens previous security bounds by removing reliance on unproven conjectures and achieving a round-independent complexity bound.
main_problem: The paper proves the impossibility of constructing perfectly complete quantum key agreement protocols (QKA) using only black-box access to quantumly secure one-way functions.
main_result: It demonstrates that an eavesdropper can recover the shared secret key with certainty using a polynomial number of classical oracle queries, specifically $O((q_A + q_B)^5)$.
method: The proof utilizes the quantum polynomial method over the Boolean cube and relies on establishing that the probability distributions associated with different keys must have pairwise disjoint supports.
model_or_system: The analysis is conducted in the Quantum Random Oracle Model (QROM) within a Quantum Computation with Classical Communication (QCCC) framework. Parties exchange only classical messages and query an oracle $H_z$.
key_observables: The shared secret key, which must be uniquely determined by the eavesdropper.
important_parameters: The maximum number of quantum queries allowed for Alice ($q_A$) and Bob ($q_B$), which dictate the complexity bound.
main_assumptions: The protocol must achieve perfect completeness ($\Pr[K_A = K_B] = 1$). The model restricts communication to classical messages, disallowing pre-shared entanglement or quantum channels.
paper_structure: The paper builds the argument by first establishing polynomial representations for the protocol's probability structure (Transcript Rectangularity), then using properties of disjoint supports to limit candidate keys, and finally employing a decision tree search over these candidates to derive the query complexity bound.
why_interesting: While focused on QKD/QKA security proofs rather than physical AMO systems, the underlying mathematical techniques involving polynomial methods and information-theoretic security bounds are fundamental tools in quantum information theory that inform secure communication protocols relevant to quantum networking.
